J’ai rencontré Clara* peu avant les élec: I met Clara* shortly before the U.S. election in 2024. She had arrived in Montréal a few months earlier, and a community leader who supports immigrants through the integration process put her in touch with me. He was following her situation closely because of her family’s significant needs, both here in Montréal and in Mexico.
Clara est mère de cinq enfants, dont qua: Clara is a mother of five, four of whom had to stay behind in Mexico with her husband. They too are looking for a way to escape the violence plaguing Guanajuato, the city where the family lived until May 2024. Clara arrived in Montréal with Jesús*, her eldest son, who has several medical conditions and cannot move from the waist down.
En apprenant son histoire, je n’ai pu m’: As I learned her story, I couldn’t help thinking about the rise of anti-immigration rhetoric in Canada and the United States. South of the border, this climate of tension reached its peak with Donald Trump’s return to power and the mass deportations of immigrants he has ordered. Yet families like Clara’s, along with hundreds of thousands of others, will continue to desperately need a safe place to rebuild their lives.
Au-delà de ces considérations, j’ai auss: Beyond these considerations, I also saw in Clara’s story the strength and solidarity of a community that organizes and helps one another when the most vulnerable need it.
Here is part of her story.
Clara’s home is a little gem. Everything is spotless and perfectly tidy. The day we visited, her son Jesús was in charge of making sure everything smelled fresh. He tells us himself with a proud smile: “I’m the one who cleaned.” The apartment, on the ground floor of a building in Côte-des-Neiges, has little furniture, but just enough for us to sit down and have the coffee Clara made as soon as we arrived. With her big smile contrasting with the dark circles under her eyes, she radiates something gentle and overflows with warmth.
Elle et son fils sont arrivés au Canada: She and her son arrived in Canada on May 30, 2024, from Guanajuato, Mexico, leaving part of their family behind. Clara and her husband, married for 19 years, have five children, but only Clara and Jésus were able to make the trip to Montréal.
Jésus, qui est âgé de 18 ans, a une cond: Jésus, who is 18, has a complex medical condition – spina bifida and hydrocephalus – that prevents him from moving from the waist down. He depends entirely on his mother for basic care, though that doesn’t stop him from lending a hand to keep the house spotless.
Clara peut aussi compter sur le soutien: Clara can also count on the support of a network of contacts she has built in less than a year in Montréal. Friends and neighbours help her with things related to Jesús and step in if she has to leave the house for longer than usual. For her and for Jesús, the community has become indispensable.
« Nous sommes – ou plutôt : nous étions: “We are – or rather, we were – merchants,” Clara explains. “We ran a business for 17 years: a taco stand that let us support ourselves for a long time and manage Jesus’s illness,” she says with deep nostalgia as she recalls what her life was like before she became, along with her eldest son, an asylum seeker in Canada.
« Mais en février [2024], ils ont commen: “But in February [2024], they started asking us for money so that we could keep selling our tacos,” she continues.
Cette forme d’extorsion – appelée <em>el: This form of extortion – called el cobro de plaza, but also known as vacuna or cobrar piso – involves demanding money from merchants and business owners on a recurring basis. In Guanajuato, one of the most violent cities in Mexico, this kind of crime is committed by criminal organizations linked to drug cartels.
« Ils ont commencé par nous demander 500: “They started by asking us for 500 pesos a day (about $35). To give you an idea, we sold each taco for 13 pesos (about $0.90). I know that doesn’t sound like a lot of money, but you have to understand that we lived off what we sold. Having someone at home with a chronic illness, who needs a lot of medication, diapers and appointments with specialists, complicates everything,” says Clara.
Très vite, les criminels ont doublé leur: Very quickly, the criminals doubled their demand, insisting on 1,000 pesos a day ($70). “On a good day, we managed to sell about 1,400 pesos’ worth ($98). So when they asked us for more money, we started borrowing.”
Cette extorsion, la <em>plaza</em>, n’es: This extortion, the plaza, is not the only reason that pushed Clara to close her taco stand and immigrate to Canada with Jesús. The threats were getting more and more serious, and past traumas resurfaced, including the murder of her sister-in-law four years ago and that of the mother of one of her children’s classmates. They led her to make the difficult decision to pack two backpacks and leave with her eldest son in search of an unknown land where they would be safer.
<strong>«</strong> Nous savions qu’à un: “We knew that at some point we wouldn’t be able to pay them anymore and that we would end up like my sister-in-law... That’s when I said, ‘Let’s go to Canada!’” she says, wringing her hands.
Les rapports établis sur la violence au: Reports on violence in Mexico confirm what Clara describes. According to the Mexico Peace Index, produced by the Institute for Economics & Peace, the rate of activity carried out by organized crime in Guanajuato has risen by 632 per cent over the past eight years. In January 2025 alone, the Secretariat of Security and Citizen Protection recorded more than 216 homicides in the city.
<strong>« </strong>Nous venons d’un endr: “We come from a place where people are killed for nothing. Yes, it’s the place where we grew up and where we lived for many years. We even know our extortionists... But everything has changed. Now the cartels recruit kids. Chamaquitos**… They’re getting younger and younger,” Clara laments.
Le plan initial de Clara était d’immigre: Clara’s initial plan was to immigrate to Canada with her whole family. That wasn’t possible because only she and Jesús had U.S. visas, since Jesús receives treatment for his medical condition in Chicago.
Rappelons également qu’à la fin de févri: It should also be noted that in late February 2024, the Canadian government reinstated the visa requirement for Mexicans wishing to visit the country. However, the regulations in place allow Mexicans who hold a U.S. visa to travel to Canada by simply obtaining an electronic travel authorization (eTA).
Clara et Jesús sont donc arrivés à l’aér: Clara and Jesús therefore arrived at Trudeau airport in Montréal in May 2024 with $200 in their pockets – money they had scraped together by pawning the little they owned – and two backpacks. She remembers perfectly that it was still dark out, that she had trouble communicating with the immigration officers and that, to her great surprise, she turned out to be stronger than she thought she was.
<strong>« </strong>J’avais très peur qua: “I was very scared when we arrived. [The immigration officers] asked me what I was doing in Montréal, whether I knew anyone, how much money I had and where I was going to spend the night. They gave me a piece of paper with an address and recommended that I go there. I said I had come to ask for refuge,” she says.
Après cette première étape migratoire, <: After this first stage of the journey, “I tried to be strong, but I asked myself: ‘And now, what do we do? Where do we go?’” she continues.
<strong>« </strong>Je voyais des gens do: “I saw people sleeping at the airport, so I thought that’s what we could do. Then a man came up to me and spoke to me in English. He was a taxi driver. I showed him the paper the officer had given me and told him I only had $200. He said he would drive me, and that’s when I found all my strength, because I managed to carry Jesús, who is already an adult, and get him into the car. That’s where our adventure began.”
Le lendemain, après avoir passé la nuit: The next day, after spending the night in a meeting room in a place whose name escapes Clara, she and Jesús were able to move into a hotel room and receive help from a social worker at <l1>Praida</l1>.
Avec l’aide de traducteurs et les 120 $: With the help of translators and the $120 she had left after paying for the taxi from the airport, she managed to get a cell phone number and buy essentials, such as diapers for her son.
Clara a progressivement surmonté sa peur: Clara gradually overcame her fear. She quickly began looking for resources for asylum seekers. That is how she was able to get help from <l1>INICI</l1>, an organization that assists newcomers.
Avec Praida, elle a commencé à comprendr: With Praida, she began to understand her rights as an asylum seeker while learning to get around the city by public transit. “Praida gave me two OPUS cards, and that’s how we got around Montréal,” she says proudly. She and her son also began receiving social assistance: $820 each.
Les premiers mois de Clara et de Jesús à: Clara and Jesús’s first months in Montréal were a roller coaster. Although she felt that everything was moving forward, her heart and mind were still in Mexico, because her four other children, aged 3, 8, 11 and 16, along with her husband, were going through extreme hardship as they tried to flee the violence in Mexico.
« Ils ont été dans plusieurs villes, de: “They’ve been in several cities, from León to Comanja de Corona, by way of Mexico City and Jalisco. They kept moving, with the help of contacts and loans. They suffered a lot, went hungry and often didn’t have a proper place to sleep,” she explains, without giving further details for fear for their lives.
Mais l’angoisse qu’a constamment éprouvé: But the anguish Clara constantly felt did not stop her from seeking help in Montréal. Immigration officers told her that she and her son had to leave the hotel on July 10. With that deadline in mind, she began searching for an apartment across the city.
Si pour un demandeur d’asile il est comp: If finding a place to live is complicated for an asylum seeker because of the requirements imposed in the middle of a housing crisis – one that some politicians have tried to pin on immigrants – for Clara the difficulty was twofold, because Jesús’s particular needs made many of the options she found unworkable.
Une autre travailleuse sociale, cette fo: Another social worker, this time from Aide aux immigrants à Montréal (<l1>AIEM</l1> ), joined her search for housing and found a basement apartment, but one with ramp access. On July 8, a month and eight days after arriving in Montréal, Clara and Jesús moved into their first apartment, in Mercier-Est.
Ce logement était bien, explique Clara,: The place was fine, Clara explains, but it wasn’t suited to Jesús’s needs. The bathroom, for example, was inaccessible to him.
Parallèlement, la mère a cherché des moy: At the same time, the mother looked for ways to bring her family together in Canada. “I contacted a lawyer, whom a new friend helped me pay. He explained that the process could take five to six years, even though efforts are being made to speed things up,” she laments. Yet she immediately regains her optimism. “Hope is the last thing you lose,” she says.
<strong>Établie et pleine d’espoir, mais: Settled and hopeful, but with a void
L’élan de Clara est indéniable. Comme ta: Clara’s drive is undeniable. Like so many asylum seekers, she finds her strength in necessity. Although she hasn’t yet started looking for a job, she has begun all the steps needed for her son to receive the medical care he needs in Montréal. She hopes to be able to work once those steps have progressed enough.
Maintenant établie à Côte-des-Neiges, el: Now settled in Côte-des-Neiges, she is closer to the Montreal General Hospital, which makes it easier to book appointments. At home, CLSC workers come to help her bathe Jesús.
« En plus, j’ai la bonne compagnie des v: “On top of that, I have the good company of my neighbours, including Mexican families, who helped me find a sense of belonging and offered me support,” she says, adding that she has seen “that there is mutual aid among immigrants – we trade support and contacts to overcome difficulties.”
Avec l’aide du réseau communautaire qu’e: With the help of the community network she has built, Clara organized a traditional Mexican pozole to raise funds to buy Jesús a new wheelchair. Although the fundraiser didn’t bring in as much as she had hoped, she values the neighbourly ties and the sense of community with the people around her.
Jesús progresse également dans son adapt: Jesús is also making progress adapting to Montréal. Like his mother, the young man – who constantly wears a radiant smile – is excited to start studying French soon in a class adapted for people with special needs. He was supposed to start francization classes the week of February 10, but Montréal’s historic snowfall delayed his start. “It’s very complicated because of the wheelchair,” says his mother.
Au Mexique, les choses ne s’améliorent p: In Mexico, things aren’t getting better for Clara’s family. Her husband recently suffered from colitis and had to be hospitalized, while the children have been looking for ways to cope with the absence of their mother and big brother.
« La petite de huit ans m’a récemment di: “My eight-year-old recently told me she doesn’t want to grow up because by the time she sees me again, she’ll already be a teenager. I told her not to look at it that way, to be patient and to pray to God that all this passes quickly. She cries a lot. Then I tell her a story and she falls asleep,” she says, her voice breaking.
« Parfois, je me demande si tout cela en: “Sometimes I wonder if it’s all really worth it. I feel guilty because we’re in a comfortable and, above all, safe place, while they keep suffering over there. Two weeks ago, they found the head and body of a friend who worked near our taco stand. All this violence goes on while the cartels recruit young people. My children tell me they don’t want to stay in Mexico... That’s what’s hard.”
Malgré tant de défis et de difficultés,: Despite so many challenges and hardships, Clara keeps a positive, even grateful, attitude. She has no idea when she will receive an answer from Immigration Canada about her and her son’s asylum claim, but she feels supported by her community. It is a strength that pushes her forward, in the hope of soon being able to hug her husband and her four other children.
